_comment: The Outlaw Lord's villain (Expansion 6 D.3, docs/ADVENTURES.md §6.2): the gang's captain, cunning or cruel; his moves (an omen, a warning nailed to your door, a test on the road) and his boss template (met before his hideout he breaks off; in it, phase two: his men come running).

first_words: "I wondered when you'd come," says {villain}, and does not get up. "Sit. We can do this the clever way, or the other way."
"Do come in," says {villain}, pouring two cups. "Drink. We have been expecting you since the ford, and there is no hurry."
"You are clever," says {villain}. "I like that. Clever people can be reasoned with, and the others must be killed." {His} blade lies on the table within reach, and {he} has not touched it.
"{town} pays you, I suppose," says {villain_short}. "{town} pays me more. Set your sword down and let us count the difference."
"Ah," says {villain}. "The stranger. I have heard a good deal about you, and not all of it was flattering. Stay your hand. I will name my price before you name yours."
"You went to a great deal of trouble to come here," says {villain_short}, and smiles. "I should like to know it was worth it. Tell me what you want of me."
{villain_short} does not rise. "{gang} has fed on this country for years because I am patient, friend. I am patient now. Speak, and then we shall see how the evening goes."
omens: A rag in the gang's colour is tied round the milestone here, fresh, knotted the way the carters say means you have been seen.
A new toll-board stands at the ford, neatly lettered: one tenth of the load, and safe passage. Nobody has dared tear it down.
A purse hangs from a branch at the roadside, tied with a ribbon, and it is empty. Whoever left it wanted you to find it empty.
Pennies are pressed into the mud of the road, one for every wagon that passed this morning. Not one of the wagons was touched.
A tally is scored on the gatepost with a knife: rows of strokes grouped in fives, a cross beside every fifth. It is in a neat hand.
A clean white cloth lies folded on the milestone with a stone upon it, like a table laid for guests.
Somebody has raked the road smooth here. In the middle of it a single set of footprints leads away into the trees.
A tin cup hangs from a stake at the wayside, and in it a coin, and a scrap of paper: for the stranger's trouble.
A feather in the gang's colour is stuck in the bark of the roadside oak at the height of a rider's eye, fresh, as if put there while you watched.
A line of stones crosses the road, a cart's width apart, each with a pebble set on top. A count, or a game. The carters will not step over it.

first_words: "You've cost me men," says {villain}. "I'm going to take it out of you slowly."
"I hear you hurt my people," says {villain}. "I will hurt yours. I have not yet decided which of them first."
"I have a rope for you," says {villain_short}, "and a branch picked out."
"You walked in at my door," says {villain}. "It will be the last thing you do on your own feet."
{villain_short} laughs, short and ugly. "Another who thinks {gang} can be stopped. They all die just the same."
"I took {town}'s wagons, and I took {town}'s sleep," says {villain}. "Now I will take your head, and send it down the road in a sack."
"No bargains," says {villain_short}, and draws. "You have counted my men. Now I will count yours, one at a time."
omens: A carter hangs from the oak at the crossroads, a board round his neck: HE DID NOT PAY.
A burned wagon sits in the ditch, the axle charred through, the ox still yoked to it. The crows have had the best of the ox.
A hand is nailed to the milestone, palm out, with a ring on the third finger. The flies are thick on it.
Stakes are driven along the verge, and a head sits on each of the first three, hats still on. The fourth stake waits.
A mule lies dead in the road with its throat opened, and a board hung round its neck: THIS ONE PAID LATE.
The ground by the ford is trampled to red mud. There is a child's shoe in it, and nothing else, and nobody left to ask.
A signpost is hung with strips of coloured cloth, torn from the coats of those who did not pay. The wind makes them dance.
Hoofprints lead off the road to a drover's cottage. The door is broken in and the thatch burned, and a dog lies dead in the yard.
Carters' whips are nailed in a row to a gate, handles out, each with a name cut in the leather. One of the cuts is still wet.
A broken wheel is lashed upright at the roadside, a shirt tied to the spokes, stiff with something dark. The gang's mark is cut in the hub.

lines: "To me! To me, you dogs!" the captain roars, and two more of the gang come running out of the dark with blades out.
The captain puts two fingers to the mouth and whistles, shrill and long, and from the dark come two more blades.
"Up! Up, all of you!" the captain shouts, and from the passage behind two of the gang come running, still pulling on boots.
A horn sounds close behind the captain, and two of the gang drop out of the shadows with steel drawn, answering the call.
The captain has seen enough. A whistle, and the whole band melts into the trees as if it had never been.
The captain lifts a hand, and the gang is gone: a rustle in the bracken, a scatter of hooves, and nothing. The captain goes with it.
A short high whistle from the captain, and the whole band slips away through the undergrowth. By the time you move, you are alone.
The captain weighs you, and weighs the odds, and takes the band off into the dusk with a wave of the hand. Not yet, the wave says.
